title: Wired and Wireless Networks
intro: An independent 10–15 minute catch-up with feedback, unlimited retries and 80% mastery.

questions.prompt: More users share a limited network link. What may happen?
Which network medium uses radio waves rather than a physical cable?
questions.feedback: Wi-Fi sends and receives information using radio.

stages.label: Learn
stages.lead: Read and follow the new material.

blocks.title: Copper cables
blocks.text: Wired copper connections carry electrical signals and are affordable, but have speed/distance limits.

blocks.title: Fibre-optic cables
blocks.text: Fibre carries pulses of light, supporting high rates and long distances; installation can be more costly.

blocks.title: Wireless connections
blocks.text: Wi-Fi uses radio waves so devices can move without cables, but connections may experience interference and interception.

blocks.title: Choose a connection
blocks.text: Use the scenario: high bandwidth, cost, mobility, length of cable, interference and security matter.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: The connection is between buildings over a substantial distance. Fibre uses light pulses [1] and is suitable for high-speed, longer-distance links [1]. Copper carries electrical signals [1] and has greater limitations on speed/distance for such a link [1]. Two contrasts, each explained in context, make four points.

items: Wired connection — A link using a physical cable.
Copper cable — Transmission medium carrying electrical signals.
Fibre optic — Transmission medium carrying signals as light.
Wireless connection — Communication without a connecting cable, often radio.
Interference — Unwanted signals disrupting data transmission.
Encryption — Scrambling data so unintended recipients cannot read it without the key.
